diff_user.system: You are optimizing a Go function. Popcount(xs []uint64) int must return the total number of set bits across all words of xs. Each candidate is scored by running it in giri, a Go SSA interpreter, on 50 test vectors. It must return the reference result on every vector, and leave xs unchanged. Among correct candidates, a lower abstract cost (the number of SSA instructions executed over all vectors) scores higher, and any correct candidate scores above any incorrect one. The only import allowed is math/bits. Keep the function's name and signature.
responses:
## Proposed change: reslice the 16-word block once

The current program has the same abstract cost (3567) across all four structurally different attempts. That suggests the cost is dominated by the per-word `OnesCount64` calls and the length dispatch, and that the rewrites so far haven't touched the parts that vary. The one lever I can see is the bounds checks in the hot 16-word block: each `xs[k]` carries its own index check, and `xs[16:]` is taken as a separate reslice.

Reslicing once to `b := xs[:16]` gives the compiler a slice of statically known length 16. The constant indices `b[0]`..`b[15]` then need only the single check from the reslice, and the recursive call still uses `xs[16:]`. This removes repeated bounds-check work from the hot path without changing the dispatch structure or the result.

This is an untested guess at the cost model. If the interpreter already eliminates these checks, the score will stay flat, but it's a low-risk edit that keeps the correctness and the aliasing behaviour (the function never writes to `xs`).
